extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate mathematics students learning proofs, functions, and introductory calculus/analysis
extracted.subtask_short: writing proofs about functions and limits
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and formal criteria for proving and reasoning about functions (injective, surjective, bijective), compositions, inverses, images/preimages, the pigeonhole principle, and epsilon–delta limits in undergraduate proof-focused mathematics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Injective (one-to-one) function criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: A function f is injective if f(x)=f(y) implies x = y (i.e., distinct domain elements map to distinct codomain elements).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To prove injectivity, show f(x)=f(y) => x=y (direct approach) or use a contrapositive approach as in Example 12.6: assume f(m,n)=f(k,ℓ) and deduce coordinate equalities (subtract equations, etc.). Anti-pattern: demonstrating only that two specific inputs map to different outputs does not prove injectivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surjective (onto) function criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: A function f : A → B is surjective if for every b in B there exists a in A with f(a)=b.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To prove surjectivity, take an arbitrary b in the codomain and construct or solve for a preimage a (solve equations, invert formulas). Example guidance: form equations f(x)=b and solve (e.g., linear system for Z×Z → Z×Z). Anti-pattern: showing that many elements are hit but failing to handle an arbitrary codomain element.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bijective function and inverse relation criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: A function f : A → B is bijective iff its inverse relation f^{-1} (obtained by swapping coordinates) is itself a function from B to A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equivalently, f is bijective exactly when f^{-1} is a function; then f^{-1}∘f = i_A and f∘f^{-1} = i_B. To compute inverses: write y=f(x), swap x and y, solve for y; always check by composition. Anti-patterns: attempting to form f^{-1} when f is not injective (gives repeated first coordinates) or not surjective (missing first coordinates).

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition existence condition
rubrics_metrics.description: The composition g∘f is defined only when the codomain of f equals (or at least is a subset of) the domain of g.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be careful about domain/codomain matching—Example 12.9 shows composition is not defined when codomain of f ≠ domain of g. Note: it's sufficient that the range of f be contained in the domain of g.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition associativity
rubrics_metrics.description: Composition of functions is associative: if f:A→B, g:B→C, h:C→D then (h∘g)∘f = h∘(g∘f).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof strategy: evaluate both sides at an arbitrary x∈A and show both equal h(g(f(x))). Use this to reorder parentheses freely in multi-compositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition preserves injectivity and surjectivity
rubrics_metrics.description: If f and g are injective then g∘f is injective. If f and g are surjective then g∘f is surjective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proofs: for injectivity, g(f(x))=g(f(y)) ⇒ f(x)=f(y) ⇒ x=y. For surjectivity, for any c∈C find b with g(b)=c (g surjective), then a with f(a)=b (f surjective), so g(f(a))=c. Anti-pattern: assuming g∘f injective implies each factor is injective (not necessarily true in reverse).

rubrics_metrics.name: Identity function properties
rubrics_metrics.description: The identity function i_A : A→A defined by i_A(x)=x is bijective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use i_A to express inverse identities: for a bijection f, f^{-1}∘f = i_A and f∘f^{-1} = i_B. Identity is trivially injective and surjective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inverse function computation recipe
rubrics_metrics.description: To find f^{-1}: write y=f(x), interchange variables to get x=f(y), then solve for y to obtain y=f^{-1}(x).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After algebraic inversion, verify by computing f^{-1}(f(x))=x (and f(f^{-1}(x))=x). Examples: invertible polynomial or rational formulas; track domains and codomains when swapping variables.

rubrics_metrics.name: Image and preimage definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: For f:A→B and X⊆A, f(X) = {f(x): x∈X} ⊆ B. For Y⊆B, the preimage f^{-1}(Y) = {x∈A : f(x)∈Y} ⊆ A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cautions: X and Y are subsets (not elements). f^{-1}(Y) (preimage set) is meaningful even when f has no inverse function. Distinguish between f({s}) = {f(s)} and f(s)=value. Examples illustrate preimages yielding multiple domain elements mapping to the same codomain element.

rubrics_metrics.name: Image/preimage set identities (Theorem 12.4)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some equalities become strict inclusions in general (see exercises). Use these identities for set-theoretic manipulations; counterexamples show where equality fails (e.g., f(W∩X) may be strictly contained).

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterizations of injectivity and surjectivity via image/preimage
rubrics_metrics.description: f is injective iff for all X⊆A we have X = f^{-1}(f(X)). f is surjective iff for all Y⊆B we have f(f^{-1}(Y)) = Y.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These give set-theoretic tests for injectivity/surjectivity. Use them to prove or disprove injectivity/surjectivity by checking the stated equalities on arbitrary subsets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pigeonhole principle (function version)
rubrics_metrics.description: Suppose A and B are finite sets and f:A→B is any function. (1) If |A| > |B| then f is not injective. (2) If |A| < |B| then f is not surjective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use counting arguments: more pigeons than holes forces a collision (non-injectivity); fewer pigeons than holes forces empty holes (non-surjectivity). Examples: subsets sums and hair-count application demonstrate non-constructive existence via pigeonhole.

rubrics_metrics.name: Triangle inequality and corollaries
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret as distances on the number line; apply to manipulate and bound absolute-value expressions in proofs (e.g., in epsilon–delta estimates).

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit (epsilon–delta) precise definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Given f:X→R and c∈R, lim_{x→c} f(x) = L means: for every ε>0 there exists δ>0 such that 0 < |x−c| < δ implies |f(x)−L| < ε.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Symbolically: ∀ε>0 ∃δ>0 (0<|x−c|<δ ⇒ |f(x)−L|<ε). Always exclude x=c in the implication (0<|x−c|) because f(c) may be undefined. Also ensure there exists some δ>0 with (c−δ,c+δ) subset of the domain (so the statement is meaningful).

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategies for proving limits (constructive delta selection)
rubrics_metrics.description: Typical method: assume ε>0, algebraically manipulate |f(x)−L| to factor out |x−c| if possible, then choose δ as a function of ε (often δ = min(1, ε/K) after bounding other factors).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: For linear functions |3x+4−10| = 3|x−2| pick δ = ε/3. For polynomials, bound auxiliary factors by restricting δ ≤ 1 (e.g., ensure |x+2| < 5) then choose δ = min(1, ε/25). Common anti-pattern: picking δ without controlling other x-dependent factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proving a limit does not exist (contradiction / sidewise behavior)
rubrics_metrics.description: To show lim_{x→c} f(x) does not exist, assume a limit L exists and derive a contradiction, often by finding sequences or points approaching c from different sides giving distinct limiting behaviors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: piecewise functions with differing left/right limits (Example 13.3) or oscillatory behavior like sin(1/x) near 0 (Example 13.4). Use carefully chosen sample points within any δ to contradict the ε-condition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Domain neighborhood requirement for limits
rubrics_metrics.description: The limit lim_{x→c} f(x) makes sense only if there exists δ>0 such that f is defined on (c−δ,c)∪(c,c+δ) (i.e., on a punctured neighborhood of c).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If no such punctured neighborhood exists (e.g., function undefined on one side of c), then the epsilon–delta limit statement is meaningless or the limit does not exist in the two-sided sense. Example: √x at 0 is not defined for x<0, so the two-sided limit at 0 is not meaningful without domain adjustments.
